rationale: Sirach identifies Joshua son of Nun as Moses' successor. Numbers records Moses presenting Joshua before Eleazar and the congregation, laying hands on him, and giving him authority so Israel will obey him.

Sirach praises Joshua for giving Israel its inheritance after warfare. Joshua's narrative closes the conquest summary by saying that he gave the land to Israel as tribal inheritances and that the land ceased being at war.

Sirach recalls Joshua stretching out an armed hand against cities. At Ai, Joshua stretches his hand toward the city and the ambush rises to capture it; the target specifies a javelin, whereas Sirach calls the weapon a sword.
Sirach characterizes Joshua's campaigns as the Lord's wars. Joshua's account of the exceptional day at Gibeon expressly says that the Lord fought alongside Israel.

Sirach's extended day and restrained sun recall Joshua's request that the sun stand over Gibeon. The narrative says that the sun did not advance toward sunset for a full day and that God listened to Joshua.

Sirach joins Joshua's appeal to the Lord with an answer through hailstones. Joshua's narrative describes the Lord hurling hailstones on the fleeing enemies, records Joshua speaking to the Lord, and concludes that God listened to a human being.

Sirach places the enemies' destruction on a descent. Joshua locates the rout and heaven-sent hailstones on the descent of Horonin, giving a concrete setting for this recollection of the Lord's warfare.

Sirach names Joshua and Caleb as the two who opposed the assembly's rebellious grumbling. Numbers records them tearing their garments, praising the land, and urging the congregation not to desert the Lord or fear its inhabitants.

Sirach recalls the exceptional preservation of Joshua and Caleb for entry into the promised land. Numbers excludes the grumbling generation from entry but expressly excepts these two men; their survival is the shared point, without deriving Sirach's troop figure from this passage.

Sirach says that Joshua and Caleb alone survived from the earlier generation for the inheritance. The later census explicitly reports that none of the men registered in the wilderness remained except Joshua and Caleb.

Sirach praises Caleb's enduring strength, mountain inheritance, and descendants' possession. Caleb says that he is still strong at eighty-five, asks for the mountain, recalls the promise to his children, and receives Hebron.
Sirach's account of Caleb's offspring inheriting land recalls the Lord's promise that Caleb would enter the land and his seed would inherit it because he followed the Lord.

Sirach draws the lesson that following the Lord is good from Caleb's experience. Joshua explains Caleb's lasting possession of Hebron by his following the command of the Lord, making the same connection between his loyalty and inheritance.

Sirach honors judges who did not turn from the Lord. Judges describes the Lord raising judges and remaining with them to rescue Israel, while distinguishing the people's recurring abandonment of the Lord after a judge died.

Sirach commemorates faithful judges as a group. Hebrews names Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah among those remembered for faith and victories, offering another retrospective honoring of these leaders.

Sirach wishes that the judges' bones would flourish again; Isaiah describes bones springing up like vegetation when the Lord's servants rejoice. The shared image expresses renewed flourishing without requiring both passages to describe the same event.
The wish that honored predecessors' bones flourish again from their place recurs nearly word for word. Sirach applies it here to the judges and later to the twelve prophets.
Sirach credits Samuel with anointing Israel's rulers. In the narrative whose preceding verses identify Saul, Samuel pours oil on him and declares that the Lord has anointed him ruler over Israel.
Sirach's reference to Samuel anointing rulers also corresponds to David's anointing. The Lord instructs Samuel to anoint David, and Samuel anoints David among his brothers.
Sirach describes Samuel judging the assembly. The narrative says that he judged Israel throughout his life and lists the circuit of places where he carried out that responsibility.

Sirach joins Samuel's prophetic reliability with recognition of his words. The narrative says none of his words fell to the ground and that all Israel recognized him as a faithful prophet to the Lord.

Sirach recalls Samuel appealing to the Lord amid an enemy threat while offering a suckling lamb. The narrative supplies all three details: the enemy advance, Samuel's prayer for Israel, and the nursing lamb offered as a whole burnt offering.
Sirach's heavenly thunder and great divine voice recall the Lord thundering with a great voice against the attacking foreigners while Samuel offered the sacrifice.

Sirach attributes the defeat of hostile rulers to Samuel's period. The narrative describes enemy satraps advancing, their defeat during Samuel's intercession, and the Lord humbling the foreigners throughout Samuel's days; it does not name the Tyrian leaders mentioned by Sirach.

Sirach recalls Samuel's public declaration that he had taken no property, not even sandals, and the absence of accusations. The narrative preserves his challenge before the Lord and His anointed, explicitly mentions a sandal, and records the people's confirmation that he had taken nothing.

Sirach recalls Samuel speaking from the earth after death to announce the king's end. The narrative identifies the figure rising from the earth as Samuel and records his warning that Saul and his sons would fall and Israel's camp would be handed to its enemies.
Sirach places Nathan's prophetic activity in David's reign. The narrative names Nathan as the prophet to whom David speaks and then records the Lord's word coming to Nathan with a message for David.

Sirach compares David's selection from Israel with fat set apart from a peace offering. Leviticus directs the removal of specified fat from the sacrifice of deliverance and its offering on the altar, supplying the sacrificial action used in the comparison.

Sirach describes David as set apart from Israel. The anointing narrative distinguishes David from Jesse's other sons: the Lord has not chosen those presented earlier, but expressly directs Samuel to anoint David.

Sirach's image of David handling lions and bears recalls his account of protecting his father's flock. David tells Saul that he struck both lion and bear and rescued a sheep, crediting the Lord with his deliverance.

Sirach names the youthful David, his sling stone, and Goliath's defeat. The narrative describes David choosing stones, Goliath despising him as a boy, and David slinging a stone into the warrior's forehead.

Sirach credits the Lord with David's victory over the mighty warrior. David's speech to Goliath expressly invokes the Lord's name and says the Lord will deliver the enemy into his hand because the battle belongs to the Lord.

Sirach recalls David being glorified with tens of thousands. The women's victory song assigns Saul thousands and David tens of thousands, and Saul's reaction confirms that this was praise of David's achievement.

Sirach summarizes David's victories over his Philistine adversaries. The narrative describes two enemy advances after his anointing, his inquiries to the Lord, and the resulting defeats; this edition calls the opponents foreigners.
Sirach's summary of David reducing his adversaries recalls the compact narrative statement that David struck and routed the foreigners and took territory from their hand.

Sirach praises David's love for his Maker and songs of thanksgiving. The psalm's heading identifies David's song after deliverance from his enemies, and its opening expresses love for the Lord and praise of Him as helper and salvation.

Sirach describes David giving thanks and glory to the Most High. Chronicles records David publicly blessing the Lord, acknowledging His power and glory, and explicitly giving thanks and praise to His glorious name.

Sirach credits David with stationing psalm singers. Chronicles records his appointment of Levites to give thanks and praise with instruments, then names David's first appointment of praise through Asaph and his brethren.

Sirach places singers before the altar to sweeten the melodies. Chronicles' account of David's arrangements associates the priests and continual altar offerings with named singers, cymbals, trumpets, and instruments for God's songs.

Sirach joins David's ordering of festivals with praise resounding from early morning. The Levitical duties in Chronicles explicitly include morning and evening praise and the offerings for sabbaths, new moons, and feasts.
Sirach says the Lord removed David's sins. After David confesses to Nathan, the prophet expressly tells him that the Lord has put away his sin.

Sirach refers to a covenant of kings and a glorious throne given to David. Nathan's oracle promises David an established successor, enduring mercy, and a house, kingdom, and throne made sure for ever.

Sirach describes the Lord raising David's horn for ever. The psalm uses the same royal image when the Lord promises to make a horn spring up for David, with a lamp for His anointed and shame for his enemies.
Sirach introduces the son who arose after David. Kings narrates David's death and Solomon's accession to his father's throne, adding that Solomon's kingdom was firmly prepared.

Sirach connects Solomon's peace and rest on every side with building a house for God's name. Solomon's message to Hiram makes precisely that connection: David's wars prevented the work, but the Lord has now given rest and Solomon intends to build.

Sirach's peaceful reign and sanctuary building correspond to the promise David recounts for Solomon. The promised son is a man of rest, Israel receives peace in his days, and he is to build a house for the Lord's name.
Sirach praises Solomon's wisdom in youth. Solomon calls himself a little child and asks for understanding to judge; the Lord answers by giving him a discerning and wise heart.
Sirach describes Solomon as filled with understanding. Chronicles records his request for wisdom and understanding and God's explicit grant of both, supplying the parallel account of that gift.
Sirach links Solomon's wide influence with comparisons and riddles. Kings enumerates his parables and songs, describes his discourse about living things, and says peoples came to hear his wisdom.

Sirach celebrates Solomon's name reaching distant places. The queen of Sheba hears of his name in her own land, travels to question him, and declares that his discernment surpasses the report she had heard; this is a particular example of his foreign renown.

Sirach associates the countries' admiration with Solomon's songs and wise sayings. Kings enumerates his songs and parables, says that peoples came to hear his wisdom, and adds that he received gifts from kings who had heard of it.

Sirach says countries marveled at Solomon's interpretations. Chronicles describes the queen of Saba testing him with riddles, receiving explanations of every question, and declaring that the abundance of his wisdom exceeded its reputation.

Sirach portrays gold and silver as extraordinarily plentiful under Solomon. Kings describes golden vessels, silver having no value in his days, and ships bringing gold and silver, illustrating the abundance behind Sirach's metal comparisons.

Sirach compares Solomon's plentiful gold and silver with tin and lead. Chronicles similarly describes those precious metals becoming as common as stones in Jerusalem; the comparison changes, but the asserted abundance is the same.

Sirach addresses Solomon's submission to women. Kings names his many wives and concubines and says that his foreign wives turned his heart after their gods, explaining the compromise recalled by Sirach.
Sirach recalls Solomon being brought under women's power. Nehemiah likewise appeals to Solomon's example, saying that despite his greatness and God's love for him, foreign women turned him aside.

Sirach connects Solomon's failure with wrath falling on his children. Kings records the Lord's anger and the announcement that the kingdom would be torn away from Solomon's son's hand, with an exception made for David's sake.

Sirach recalls the divided dominion and a separate disobedient kingdom. Kings narrates Israel's rejection of David's house and its installation of Jeroboam as king, while Judah and Benjamin remain with David's house.

Sirach insists that the Lord's mercy and word will not fail and that David's descendants will not be wiped out. The psalm promises enduring mercy, a faithful covenant, and David's seed and throne continuing despite correction of his sons' sins.

Sirach says the Lord preserved descendants and a remnant despite royal failure. The judgment on Solomon expressly leaves his son a scepter for David's sake and for Jerusalem, illustrating preservation within the announced division.

Sirach attributes the revolt under Rehoboam to his deficient counsel. Kings shows him rejecting the elders' advice, following the young men's harsh counsel, and provoking Israel's declaration that it has no share in David's house.

Sirach's charge against Rehoboam corresponds to Chronicles' account of the same consultation and revolt: the elders recommend kindness, he follows the younger men instead, answers harshly, and the people depart to their dwellings.

Sirach says Jeroboam made Israel sin and provided a path of sin. Kings describes his golden heifers, shrines, unauthorized priestly appointments, and invented feast, explicitly calling the matter a sin.

Sirach connects Jeroboam's influence with Israel's eventual removal from its land. Kings explicitly says that Jeroboam thrust Israel away from the Lord, that Israel persisted in his sins, and that the nation was deported to Assyria.

Sirach describes accumulating wickedness until vengeance came. Kings recounts the rejected prophetic warnings, the abandonment of the commandments and idolatrous practices, and the Lord's anger and removal of Israel.

Sirach compares Elijah's prophetic word to a burning torch. Jeremiah contrasts dreams with the Lord's true word and compares that word to blazing fire; the parallel concerns the force of prophetic speech, while the prophets are different.

Sirach recalls Elijah bringing famine upon the people. Kings places a severe famine in Samaria within Elijah's ministry and records the Lord's instruction that Elijah appear before Ahab as rain is promised.

Sirach remembers the famine in Elijah's days. Jesus likewise recalls heaven being shut and a great famine during Elijah's ministry, adding the particular episode of his being sent to the widow in Sidon's territory.

Sirach says Elijah shut heaven by the Lord's word. Elijah's declaration to Ahab in Kings explicitly withholds dew and rain except through the utterance of his word, under oath by the living God of Israel.

Sirach recalls Elijah bringing down fire from heaven. Kings narrates one such occasion: Elijah appeals to the Lord with fire, fire consumes the offering and its surroundings, and the people confess the Lord as God.
Sirach's account of fire descending through Elijah is supported by Kings' two successive episodes in which fire consumes a captain and his fifty men.

Sirach associates Elijah with heaven being shut. James expressly names Elijah, describes his earnest prayer that rain cease, and contrasts the ensuing drought with the rain and fruitfulness following his later prayer.

Sirach praises Elijah's remarkable wonders. The fire answering his appeal in Kings provides a concrete example of those wonders, with the people falling before God after the offering, water, stones, and dust are consumed.
Sirach credits Elijah with raising a dead person. Kings recounts the widow's breathless son, Elijah's prayer that the child's soul return, and his presentation of the living child to his mother.

Sirach speaks of Elijah bringing down rulers from their beds. Kings records his message that the king will not leave the bed of illness but will die, followed by the king's death according to that word.

Sirach recalls Elijah's judgments against kings. In this edition's chapter 20, Elijah confronts Ahab over Naboth's vineyard and announces calamity and the destruction of his house; the passage records the judgment announced, rather than its later execution.

Sirach recalls Elijah hearing rebuke and judgment at Horeb. Kings places Elijah at Mount Horeb, records the divine question about his presence there, and gives the ensuing commands concerning Hazael, Jehu, Elisha, and the ensuing judgments.

Sirach associates Elijah with kings appointed for retribution and a prophetic successor. Kings records the Lord commissioning the anointing of Hazael and Jehu, naming Elisha as prophet in Elijah's place, and describing the succeeding agents of judgment.
Sirach recalls Elijah's fiery departure. Kings describes the chariot and horses of fire separating Elijah and Elisha, Elijah's ascent in a tumult, and Elisha watching until he sees him no more.

Sirach associates Elijah's appointed work with turning a father's heart toward a son before wrath. Malachi, at these native anchors, promises Elijah before the Lord's day and the restoration of a father's heart toward a son to avert the land's destruction.

Sirach connects Elijah with restored hearts and Israel's restoration. Luke describes John's mission in Elijah's spirit and power as turning Israel to God and fathers' hearts toward children; this relates the missions without identifying John as the same person as Elijah.

Sirach recalls Elijah's appointed restorative task. Matthew records the expectation that Elijah restore all things and Jesus' interpretation concerning John the Baptist, preserving the Gospel's own distinction between the expectation and its interpretation.

Sirach connects Elijah's departure with Elisha receiving his spirit. Kings narrates the departure, Elisha's subsequent division of the Jordan, and the prophetic community's declaration that Elijah's spirit has come to rest upon Elisha.

Sirach says Elisha was not shaken by a ruler. Kings supplies a particular example: Elisha confronts Israel's king, directs him to his father's prophets, and says he regards him only on account of Jehoshaphat.

Sirach describes Elisha's body as prophetic even after death. Kings relates a dead man's revival upon touching Elisha's bones, providing the bodily wonder behind that description without reporting a spoken prophecy from the corpse.
Sirach praises Elisha's portents during life. Kings gives the concrete example of his prayer and actions over the Shunammite woman's dead child, who opens his eyes and is returned to his mother.
Sirach distinguishes Elisha's wonders during life from those at his end. Kings' account of a man revived through contact with Elisha's bones supplies the posthumous counterpart to that contrast.

Sirach links refusal to repent with removal and scattering. Kings recounts Israel's refusal to heed prophetic warnings and its persistence in sins until the Lord removed Israel and it was deported to Assyria.

Sirach recounts the unrepentant people's removal and scattering over the earth. Deuteronomy warns of removal from the inherited land and dispersion among nations from one end of the earth to the other, supplying the corresponding covenant consequence.

Sirach describes a reduced remnant associated with David's ruling house and continuing disobedience. Kings says that only Judah remained after Israel's removal, then adds that Judah also failed to keep the Lord's commandments.
Sirach remembers Hezekiah's works bringing water into the fortified city. Kings' concluding notice expressly records his fountain and aqueduct and the bringing of water into the city.

Sirach combines Hezekiah's fortification and water works. Chronicles describes his response to the Assyrian threat through controlling nearby water, rebuilding the wall and towers, and adding an outer defensive wall.

Sirach names Sennacherib's invasion and his envoy Rabshakeh. Kings places Sennacherib's attack in Hezekiah's reign and sends the officer named Rhapsakes in this edition, with other officers and a large force, to Jerusalem.

Sirach recalls the Assyrian king's envoy and his boastful challenge to Zion. Isaiah's parallel account names Sennacherib and the envoy Rapsakes, sends him to Jerusalem, and opens his challenge by invoking the authority of the great king.

Sirach compares the people's terror to birth pains. In the same Assyrian crisis, Hezekiah's messengers describe affliction through the image of children reaching birth when the mother has no strength to deliver.
Sirach's birth-pain comparison recalls the crisis described in Isaiah: Hezekiah mourns and his messengers speak of a woman whose labor has come but who lacks strength to give birth.

Sirach recalls prayer, God's hearing, and deliverance associated with Isaiah. Chronicles explicitly joins Hezekiah and Isaiah in prayer to heaven, then recounts the Lord's intervention and Jerusalem's deliverance from Sennacherib.
Sirach says God heard the threatened people's petition. Kings records Hezekiah's plea for deliverance and Isaiah's message that the Lord has heard his prayer concerning Sennacherib.
Sirach credits an angel with striking the Assyrian camp. Kings narrates the Lord's angel striking that camp by night and the discovery of its dead in the morning.
Sirach's destruction of the Assyrian camp through an angel has a parallel account in Isaiah, which names the angel of the Lord, the Assyrian camp, and the bodies discovered the following morning.
Sirach commends Hezekiah for following David's ways. Kings identifies Hezekiah's accession and expressly assesses his conduct by everything his father David had done.

Sirach joins the backward movement of the sun with the extension of the king's life. Kings promises Hezekiah fifteen additional years and narrates Isaiah's prayer and the shadow's return ten steps as the healing sign.
Sirach's recollection of the reversed sun and prolonged life corresponds to Isaiah's account, where fifteen years are added to Hezekiah and the sun goes back up the ten steps as the promised sign.

Sirach praises Isaiah's great spirit and comfort for Zion's mourners. Isaiah presents the Lord's spirit upon the commissioned speaker and explicitly promises comfort and transformed mourning for Zion.
Sirach recalls Isaiah comforting Zion's mourners. Isaiah's repeated call to comfort God's people is directed to Jerusalem, whose humiliation is fulfilled and whose sin is loosed.

Sirach describes Isaiah disclosing hidden things before they occur. Isaiah records the Lord announcing new things before they spring up; the foresight is presented in the target as God's declaration through the prophetic text.

Sirach compares the memory of Josiah to finely prepared perfume. Ecclesiastes compares the value of a name with good oil, providing a related wisdom image in which personal reputation and good oil are brought together.

Sirach recalls Josiah turning the people back and removing abominations. Kings describes the renewed covenant, the people's participation, and his removal and destruction of objects associated with idolatrous worship.
Sirach's removal of abominations under Josiah corresponds to Chronicles' account of his seeking the Lord and cleansing Judah, Jerusalem, and other cities by destroying altars and sacred objects.
Sirach praises Josiah's directed heart and strengthening of godliness. Kings similarly singles him out for returning to the Lord with his whole heart, soul, and strength according to Moses' law.

Sirach connects Josiah's heart toward God with the people's godliness. Chronicles records his whole-hearted covenant, the people's renewed commitment, and his making those present serve the Lord throughout his days.

Sirach links Judah's royal downfall with abandonment of the law. Chronicles gives the particular final-reign example of Zedekiah's refusal to return to God, the people's breaches of faith, and their rejection of prophetic messages until wrath came.

Sirach describes Judah's strength and glory passing to foreigners. Chronicles recounts defeat by the Chaldean king, transfer of temple and royal treasures to Babylon, and the survivors' servitude there.

Sirach recalls the city of the sanctuary being burned and its streets made desolate. Kings records the burning of the Lord's house, the king's house, and Jerusalem's houses, followed by removal of the remaining people.
Sirach's burning and desolation of Jerusalem correspond to Chronicles' destruction of the Lord's house, city wall, and citadels, followed by deportation of the survivors.

Sirach recalls Jeremiah's consecration in the womb and commission to destroy, build, and plant. Jeremiah's opening call explicitly places consecration before birth and appoints him to uproot, demolish, destroy, build, and plant.

Sirach praises Ezekiel's vision of glory. Ezekiel describes the throne-like form, its radiance, and the rainbow-like brightness, explicitly identifying this as the appearance of the likeness of the Lord's glory.

Sirach associates Ezekiel's glorious vision with the cherubim's chariot. Ezekiel describes the cherubim rising with wheels, the Lord's glory mounting them, and his recognition that these are the creatures seen at the river Chebar.

Sirach speaks of God remembering enemies in a rainstorm. Ezekiel's oracle against Gog describes divine judgment through flooding rain and hailstones. The supported connection is this specific storm-judgment image; the passage does not establish that Sirach is identifying this particular oracle.

Sirach honors the twelve prophets for comforting Jacob and sustaining hope of redemption. Zechariah supplies a particular example: the Lord answers with comforting words and promises compassion, rebuilding, and renewed mercy for Jerusalem and Zion.

Sirach prays that the twelve prophets' bones flourish from their place. The earlier praise of the judges likewise asks that their bones flourish from their place, repeating the memorial prayer for another group of Israel's honored ancestors.

Sirach compares Zerubbabel to a signet on the right hand. Haggai's promise names Zerubbabel, calls him God's chosen servant, and says God will make him like a signet; Haggai does not specify the hand.

Sirach credits Joshua son of Jozadak and Zerubbabel with rebuilding the Lord's house. Ezra names the corresponding leaders as Iesous son of Iosedek and Zorobabel son of Salathiel and records their beginning to rebuild God's house with prophetic assistance.
Sirach remembers Nehemiah for restoring the fallen walls. Nehemiah records the wall's completion and the surrounding nations' recognition that God brought the work to completion.

Sirach credits Nehemiah with restored walls and gates. Nehemiah records the built wall, the setting up of doors, and arrangements to close and guard them. This supports the wall and gate details; the adjacent verse 7:4 still says that houses had not been built.
Sirach distinguishes Enoch by his being taken from the earth. Genesis says that Enoch pleased God and was not found because God transferred him.
Sirach praises Enoch's exceptional removal from the earth. Hebrews explicitly recalls Enoch being taken away so as not to see death and connects that removal with his testimony of pleasing God.

Sirach says that care was taken of Joseph's bones. Genesis records Joseph's oath requiring his bones to be carried from Egypt at God's visitation, followed by his burial preparations and placement in a coffin.
Sirach remembers the care of Joseph's bones. Exodus records the carrying out of his oath when Moses takes those bones on Israel's departure from Egypt.
Sirach's remembrance of Joseph's bones has a further narrative counterpart in Joshua, which records their transport from Egypt and burial in Joseph's inherited portion at Shechem.

Sirach places Adam above the living creatures in his account of ancestral honor. Genesis gives humankind God's image and authority over fish, birds, cattle, the earth, and creeping things, supplying the corresponding distinction within creation.

Sirach admires Simon as he emerges from the house of the veil. Leviticus describes the priest's service within the veil and excludes others until he comes out, supplying a parallel pattern of restricted priestly entry and exit without identifying Simon's particular festival.

Sirach compares Simon's splendor to the full moon. The Song compares its praised woman to dawn and the beautiful moon; the shared celestial image describes beauty, while the persons and settings remain different.

Sirach compares Simon's splendor to a rainbow gleaming in glorious clouds. Ezekiel uses the rainbow in a rainy cloud to describe the brightness of the Lord's glory. The comparison concerns the luminous image, without equating the priest with God.

Sirach portrays Simon through lilies near water and a shoot of Lebanon. Hosea describes restored Israel receiving dew, blossoming like a lily, and putting down roots like Lebanon; both use flourishing plants and Lebanon to portray renewed beauty.

Sirach likens Simon's splendor to fire and frankincense upon a firepan. Leviticus describes the priest taking a firepan of burning coals and putting incense on the fire before the Lord, providing the particular ritual image used in the simile.
Sirach compares Simon to a fruitful olive and a towering cypress. Wisdom's earlier self-description likewise uses the cypress and stately olive; the botanical images recur with different subjects.

Sirach describes Simon's robe of glory and priestly splendor. Exodus orders Aaron's holy robe for honor and glory and enumerates garments made for priestly service, supplying the corresponding purpose of glorious priestly dress.

Sirach compares the priests surrounding the altar to Lebanon's cedars and palm trunks. The Psalm compares righteous people to palms and Lebanon's cedars and places their flourishing in the Lord's house and courts, joining the same trees with worship's setting.

Sirach depicts Aaron's sons with offerings before Israel's assembly. Leviticus places the congregation before the Lord and describes Aaron at the altar with his sons bringing him the sacrificial blood.

Sirach describes the high priest completing his altar ministry and offering. Chronicles describes the offering on the altar and the accompanying assembly's worship, singing, and trumpets continuing until the burnt offering is finished.

Sirach recounts the pouring of a drink offering before the Most High. Numbers prescribes pouring out a drink offering of strong drink to the Lord in the holy place; it supports the libation practice without specifying Sirach's altar-foundation detail.

Sirach calls the libation wine the blood of the grape. Deuteronomy likewise names wine as the blood of the grape in its account of provision, sharing the particular image although the target describes drinking rather than a libation.

Sirach describes Aaron's sons sounding trumpets as a remembrance before the Most High. Numbers assigns the trumpets to Aaron's priestly sons and expressly makes their sounding over offerings a remembrance before God.

Sirach's assembled people fall facedown to worship the Lord during the temple service. Chronicles recounts Israel's collective prostration on the pavement in response to the Lord's glory at the temple dedication; these are corresponding acts in different ceremonies.

Sirach praises the psalm singers' voices and the great sound of their melody. Chronicles describes the assembled Levitical singers and instruments joining in one voice to give thanks and praise at the sanctuary.

Sirach describes the people praying while the Lord's ceremony is completed. Luke likewise places the congregation's prayer alongside priestly service, with the multitude praying outside while the priest burns incense inside.

Sirach describes Simon coming down and raising his hands over Israel to bless them. Leviticus describes Aaron lifting his hands over the people, blessing them, and coming down after the offerings; the correspondence concerns the priestly gesture and blessing.

Sirach associates the priest's spoken blessing with the Lord's name. Numbers instructs Aaron and his sons to bless Israel, explicitly placing God's name upon them in this edition's verse 23, and gives the words of the blessing.

Sirach depicts the people bowing to receive the blessing after priestly service. Leviticus joins the priests' blessing, the appearance of divine glory, and the congregation's falling on their faces; the latter response also follows the fire consuming the offering.

Sirach calls for blessing the God who exalts human days from the womb. The Psalm acknowledges support from the womb and shelter from the mother's belly, and joins that lifelong dependence with continual praise.

Sirach petitions God for gladness of heart and peace in Israel. Romans similarly prays that God fill its hearers with joy and peace in believing, within its own setting of hope shared by Jews and Gentiles.
Sirach prays that God's mercy be entrusted to His people and that He redeem them. The Psalm connects the Lord's mercy with abundant redemption and explicitly promises the redemption of Israel.

Sirach describes the author's wisdom pouring like rain from his heart. Deuteronomy asks that the speaker's utterance be awaited like rain and his words descend like dew, using rainfall imagery for beneficial teaching without identifying the two speakers.

Sirach promises wisdom to the reader who occupies himself with these teachings and places them on his heart. The Psalm connects meditation on God's law and testimonies with becoming wiser and gaining understanding.

Sirach says that one practicing the instruction has the Lord's light as his path. The Psalm calls God's word a lamp to the feet and a light to the paths, sharing the image of divine guidance illuminating one's course.
Sirach addresses God as Lord and King and promises praise and thanksgiving to His name. The Psalm likewise addresses God as King and promises daily blessing and praise of His name.
Sirach thanks God for rescue from a slanderous tongue and false lips. The Psalm recounts an answered cry in affliction and explicitly asks for rescue from unjust lips and a deceitful tongue.

Sirach recalls gnashing teeth and the threat of being devoured by those seeking his life. The Psalm describes enemies gnashing their teeth and asks that the speaker's life be restored from their wickedness and from lions.

Sirach thanks God for rescue from surrounding fire. The Psalm recalls a community passing through fire and water before being brought to refreshment; it presents its ordeal as divine testing, while Sirach specifies a fire he did not kindle.

Sirach describes rescue from the belly of Hades. Jonah's prayer from the sea creature likewise speaks of crying from the belly of Hades and being heard by God, sharing this particular image of extremity.

Sirach recounts slander reaching a king and threatening his life. David likewise challenges Saul's acceptance of people's accusations, demonstrates his innocence, and says that Saul seeks to take his life; the parallel concerns the situation, without identifying Sirach's unnamed king as Saul.

Sirach describes being surrounded without any human helper. The Psalm joins approaching affliction with the explicit absence of anyone to help, turning that condition into an appeal for God's nearness.

Sirach remembers God's ancient mercy and rescue of those who wait for Him. The Psalm assures those who wait for God, addresses Him as Savior, and asks Him to remember His compassions and mercies from eternity.
Sirach recalls pleading for deliverance from death. The Psalm describes death's pangs and Hades' dangers and gives the ensuing cry to the Lord to rescue the speaker's soul.

Sirach asks not to be abandoned in affliction when no help is available. The Psalm likewise asks the Lord not to abandon the speaker and to attend to his aid. This supports the petition, without interpreting Sirach's distinctive address, the Father of my Lord.

Sirach's petition ends with the resolve to praise God's name continually. The Psalm likewise promises blessing at every time, continual praise in the mouth, and the shared exaltation of the Lord's name.
Sirach connects the hearing of his petition with rescue from destruction and an evil time. The Psalm similarly says that the Lord heard the poor man's cry and saved him from all his afflictions.

Sirach responds to the rescue just recounted with thanksgiving and praise. The Psalm moves from mourning transformed into gladness to a promise of praise and everlasting thanks, supplying the corresponding response to deliverance.

Sirach remembers seeking wisdom in prayer while young. Solomon's prayer similarly describes him as a little child, asks for a discerning heart, and receives the Lord's gift of a wise heart; the accounts concern different petitioners.

After recalling his youthful search, Sirach promises to seek wisdom until the end. The earlier instruction likewise spans a lifetime, beginning the choice of instruction in youth and continuing the finding of wisdom into gray-haired age.

Sirach describes his foot walking in uprightness as he traces wisdom's path. Proverbs joins instruction in wisdom with straight tracks, unhindered steps, and holding fast to discipline, sharing the portrayal of learning as a well-directed walk.

Sirach describes inclining his ear, receiving, and finding much instruction. Proverbs likewise connects receiving the commandment, the ear's obedience to wisdom, and the application of the heart with finding the knowledge of God.
Sirach gives glory to the One who gives him wisdom. Proverbs explicitly identifies the Lord as the giver of wisdom and the source of knowledge and understanding.

Sirach resolves to practice wisdom and declares that he will not be put to shame. The Psalm similarly wishes for ways directed to keeping God's ordinances and connects attention to the commandments with freedom from shame.

Sirach mourns his unwitting faults while seeking faithful practice of the law. The Psalm asks who can understand transgressions and requests cleansing of hidden faults, expressing the corresponding concern for sins beyond full awareness.

Sirach directs his soul toward wisdom and describes finding her in purity. Wisdom of Solomon joins seeking God in simplicity of heart with the warning that wisdom does not enter an evil-devising soul or dwell in a body indebted to sin.

Sirach's inward desire to seek wisdom results in acquiring a good possession. Proverbs likewise urges searching for wisdom like silver and treasure and describes the discovery of divine knowledge and the Lord's gift of wisdom.
Sirach acknowledges a tongue given by the Lord and resolves to use it for praise. The Psalm likewise connects the Lord's opening of the lips with the mouth's announcement of His praise.

Sirach invites the uninstructed to lodge in a house of instruction. Proverbs personifies Wisdom as building a house and summoning those lacking understanding to come, leave foolishness, and seek understanding.

Sirach addresses souls that thirst while lacking instruction. Isaiah likewise addresses the thirsty, invites them to freely provided nourishment, and connects listening with the soul's life and delight; the nourishment functions within an invitation to hear God.

Sirach urges hearers to acquire instruction without silver. Isaiah similarly invites those without silver to buy without silver or price and to listen for the soul's life, joining the free-acquisition image with receptive hearing.

Sirach joins putting the neck under a yoke with receiving instruction. Jesus likewise invites hearers to take His yoke and learn from Him, coupling the teaching image with rest and a light burden; this is a comparison of the invitations, not an identification of their speakers.
Sirach's final invitation places the neck beneath wisdom's yoke. The earlier exhortation likewise places the neck in her collar, urges whole-soul pursuit, and promises the discovery of her rest.

Sirach contrasts the little labor of seeking wisdom with the much rest he found. Jesus addresses those laboring and burdened with a promise of rest and describes His burden as light. Both connect the teacher's invitation with rest, while describing its demands as little labor or a light burden.

Sirach urges costly participation in instruction using silver and gold as its value imagery. Proverbs places discipline and knowledge above silver and tested gold; the comparison concerns wisdom's worth and does not turn Sirach's image into a guarantee of financial profit.
Sirach exhorts the soul to rejoice in God's mercy. The Psalm likewise promises exultation and rejoicing in divine mercy and grounds that response in rescue from humiliation and an enemy's grasp.

Sirach urges work before the appointed time and trusts God to give the reward in His time. Galatians similarly joins doing good while opportunity remains with the assurance of reaping in the proper season if one does not give up.
